title: What pagination strategies exist in JPA, how do offset and keyset pagination differ, and when does OFFSET kill performance?

s1_definition.profdef: Offset pagination uses LIMIT and OFFSET (setMaxResults/setFirstResult) to skip N rows and return the next page; it is simple but degrades linearly because the database must scan and discard all skipped rows. Keyset (cursor/seek) pagination uses a WHERE predicate on the last seen sorted key (e.g., `WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT n`), giving constant-time page fetches regardless of depth, at the cost of not supporting arbitrary jumps to a page number.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh's bank statement has a million transactions. Offset pagination is like the clerk counting past the first 900,000 entries one by one every time you ask for page 90,001 — painfully slow as you go deeper. Keyset pagination is like the clerk using a bookmark that says "last transaction you saw was number 900,000" and jumping straight to the next one — instant, no matter how deep you are.
s1_definition.oneliner: OFFSET re-scans everything you skip; keyset seeks straight to where you left off.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Offset pagination uses LIMIT and OFFSET (setMaxResults/setFirstResult) to skip N rows and return the next page; it is simple but degrades linearly because the database must scan and discard all skipped rows. Keyset (cursor/seek) pagination uses a WHERE predicate on the last seen sorted key (e.g., `WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT n`), giving constant-time page fetches regardless of depth, at the cost of not supporting arbitrary jumps to a page number.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh's bank statement has a million transactions. Offset pagination is like the clerk counting past the first 900,000 entries one by one every time you ask for page 90,001 — painfully slow as you go deeper. Keyset pagination is like the clerk using a bookmark that says "last transaction you saw was number 900,000" and jumping straight to the next one — instant, no matter how deep you are.

**One line to remember:** OFFSET re-scans everything you skip; keyset seeks straight to where you left off.

sections.s2_technical:
Offset pagination in JPA: `query.setFirstResult(page * size).setMaxResults(size)`. This becomes SQL `LIMIT size OFFSET page*size`. For page 1 it is fast. For page 90,001 of a million-row statement, the database still reads and throws away 900,000 rows before returning 10. Cost grows with offset — deep pages are slow, and new inserts can shift rows so a page may skip or repeat entries.

Keyset pagination remembers the last row's sort key. For a statement ordered by transaction id descending, the first page is `WHERE 1=1 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10`; the next page is `WHERE id < :lastSeenId ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10`. With an index on id this is an index seek — constant time regardless of depth. It is stable under concurrent inserts because it anchors on a value, not a position.

The trade-off: keyset cannot jump to "page 500" directly because it needs the key of the previous page's last row; it supports next/previous and infinite scroll naturally. Offset supports random page access, which some UIs require.

When OFFSET kills performance: large tables with deep paging (reports, exports, audit logs), especially when combined with sorting on non-indexed columns. A common production incident is a report tool that pages to the end of a 50-million-row ledger — each deep page times out. The fix is keyset pagination or restricting how deep offset paging is allowed.

Senior nuances: for composite sort keys, keyset uses a tuple comparison: `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id)`. For stable ordering you must include a unique tiebreaker (id) in the ORDER BY. Spring Data supports both: `Pageable` for offset and `Slice`/custom queries for keyset; Spring Data also has keyset support via `scrollable` APIs in recent versions.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh opens his net-banking statement and scrolls through years of transactions. Offset paging is fine for the first few pages but when he scrolls deep, each page gets slower because the database skips hundreds of thousands of rows. This is exactly where OFFSET kills performance.

Problem 2 — We want smooth infinite scroll that stays fast no matter how far back Rajesh scrolls. This is exactly keyset pagination — anchor on the last transaction id and seek forward.

Problem 3 — The operations dashboard still needs a classic page-number view for small result sets. This is where offset is acceptable.

We will build a StatementService with both offset and keyset methods and show why the deep offset is slow.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/statement-service-1.0.0.jar

# Offset page (shallow OK)
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/statement/SAV2001/offset?page=0&size=20"

# Keyset page (fast at any depth) — pass last id from previous page
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/statement/SAV2001/keyset?after=900000&size=20"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh's account SAV2001 has 1,000,000 transactions ordered by id descending.

Step 1 — Offset page 0, size 20: SQL `... ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0`. The database reads the first 20 index entries — fast.

Step 2 — Offset page 45,000, size 20: SQL `... LIMIT 20 OFFSET 900000`. The database must walk past 900,000 index entries before emitting 20. This takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds — OFFSET is killing performance.

Step 3 — Keyset first page: `WHERE id < 9223372036854775807 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`. Returns the newest 20; client remembers the last id, say 999,980.

Step 4 — Keyset next page: `WHERE id < 999980 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`. With the composite index this is a direct seek returning 20 rows in constant time — just as fast on page 45,000 as on page 1.

Step 5 — The client keeps using the last row's id as the next cursor, achieving smooth infinite scroll with stable, fast pages.

```
Hibernate: select ... order by id desc limit ? offset ?      (offset)
WARNING  Deep offset page 45000 — expect slowdown
Hibernate: select ... where account_id=? and id<? order by id desc limit ?  (keyset)
INFO  Keyset page of 20 after id 999980
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Statement request for SAV2001 (1,000,000 txns)
    │
    ├─ OFFSET PATH
    │    page 0   → LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0        → fast
    │    page 45k → LIMIT 20 OFFSET 900000   → scans 900k rows → SLOW
    │
    └─ KEYSET PATH
         first  → WHERE id < MAX  ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20
         next   → WHERE id < 999980 ...  (index seek) → CONSTANT time
         cursor = last row id
    ▼
  Fast infinite scroll regardless of depth (keyset)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Offset vs Keyset Pagination ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Iterator/Cursor: keyset carries a cursor (last id)  │
  │ Strategy: offset vs keyset chosen per use case      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: StatementService only paginates                  │
  │ O: add a new pagination strategy without changes    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       StatementService        │
  │  + offsetPage(acct,page,size) │ LIMIT/OFFSET (shallow)
  │  + keysetPage(acct,lastId,sz) │ WHERE id<last (any depth)
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 ▼ uses
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> TxnRepository │
  │  + findByAccountId(Pageable)  │
  │  + keysetPage(acct,lastId)    │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Cost model ──
  OFFSET n  → O(n) rows scanned then discarded
  KEYSET    → O(log n) index seek + O(pageSize)

  ── Call Chain (keyset) ──
  1. keysetPage(SAV2001, 999980, 20)
  2.   WHERE id<999980 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 (index seek)
  3. return 20 rows; nextCursor = last row id
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
There are two main pagination strategies and they scale very differently. Offset pagination uses limit and offset, which in JPA is setMaxResults and setFirstResult. It is trivially simple and supports jumping to any page number, but the database must physically scan and discard every row you skip, so the cost grows linearly with page depth. For the first few pages it is fine; deep into a large table it becomes a performance killer and can even time out.

Keyset pagination, also called seek or cursor pagination, instead anchors on the sort key of the last row you saw. The next page is a query with a where-clause like id less than the last seen id, ordered and limited. With an index on that key it is an index seek that returns a page in constant time regardless of how deep you are, and it is stable under concurrent inserts because it anchors on a value rather than a position. The trade-off is that you cannot jump straight to an arbitrary page number, so it suits next, previous, and infinite scroll rather than random page access.

In our National Bank of India net-banking statement, Rajesh may scroll through years of transactions. Offset paging is acceptable for the first few pages, but when he scrolls deep the database skips hundreds of thousands of rows per page and each page gets slower. So for the statement I use keyset pagination anchored on the transaction id with a supporting composite index, which keeps every page fast no matter how far back he scrolls. I reserve offset pagination for small admin result sets where a page-number UI is genuinely needed, and I cap how deep offset paging is allowed.

The senior details I add are that stable keyset ordering requires a unique tiebreaker in the order-by, typically the primary key, and that for composite sort keys like created-at plus id I use a tuple comparison so paging is correct across equal timestamps. The classic production incident this prevents is a report or export tool that offset-pages to the end of a fifty-million-row ledger and times out on every deep page; moving that to keyset pagination turns it into constant-time fetches.

---

keyPoints: Offset: OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 10 — DB still scans 10000 rows (slow)
Keyset: WHERE id > lastSeenId LIMIT 10 — index-based, constant speed
Offset: simple, supports jump to page N. Keyset: fast, forward-only
Use offset for small datasets, keyset for large datasets
